absent: Stack display, printk CPU synchronization, panic detection, and console verbosity internals outside routed fragments.
Scheduler NUMA search policy, online CPU accounting, and wrap helper edge cases.
Layouts of debug object, object descriptor, per-CPU pool, boot pool, and global pool lock.
Credential, taint, version, build identity, worker, stop, and scheduling-extension formatting details.
Slab cache lifecycle, work scheduling for deferred freeing, hash function strength, and load calculation.
Object-debug operations beyond initialization such as activation, deactivation, destruction, assertion, and object freeing.

findings.text: Externally visible stack dump entry accepting a log level tag. It determines whether the calling CPU is in panic, serializes output against other CPUs only outside panic, emits the dump, then releases serialization. Panic context bypasses cross-CPU synchronization to avoid deadlock.

Internal dump helper composes two stages: first a one-line context summary for the current task and system identity, then an architecture stack trace for the current context with no explicit task or register state supplied.

Context reporting routine emitting a tagged line with CPU number, effective user identity, process identity, truncated command name, crash-kernel load flag, taint shorthand, release and version prefix, preemption model label and build identifier, followed by conditional verbose taint, hardware description when present, and worker, stop and scheduling-extension details.

Cross-CPU print serialization uses a printk CPU synchronization primitive with interrupt state preserved across the dump. The acquire and release pair strictly bracket the dump body and are both skipped when the calling CPU is already in panic, since waiting then could deadlock.

Early boot helpers obtain and release a CPU mask allocation sized to the configured CPU capacity. Allocation draws from the boot memory pool with cache-line alignment and aborts on failure, while release returns the same sized region.

NUMA-aware spread selector folds any caller index into the online CPU count so a result is always produced, delegates to the scheduler NUMA search for the matching CPU near a node, and raises a programming warning if the outcome falls outside the valid CPU range.

Round-robin CPU selectors keep a per-CPU cursor holding the previously returned index. Each call advances with wrap over the supplied mask intersection or single mask, stores the new index only when it is valid, and by construction skips the lowest index on first use.

Public CPU selection interface offers NUMA spread by index and node plus two distributing any-CPU queries, one constrained by a single mask and one by the intersection of two masks, each returning a CPU number or an out-of-range sentinel when empty.

Character classification table holds two hundred fifty-six entries indexed by byte value. Lower entries distinguish control, spacing, punctuation, decimal digit, uppercase, lowercase and hexadecimal roles, middle entries are zero, and high entries extend punctuation and letter classes for the upper half.

Lock debugging disable entry attempts a one-way transition through a cross-dossier primitive when debugging is active. On success it raises console verbosity unless silent mode is set and reports that it performed the transition, otherwise it reports no change.
Object-debug hash width is fourteen bits, with bucket count defined as one shifted left by that width, yielding a fixed global hash table for tracked objects.

Object-debug batch unit is sixteen objects. Global capacity is sixty-four batches, its refill threshold one quarter of that, and each per-CPU cache holds eight batches, establishing a three-tier pooling hierarchy.

Address chunking aligns to the platform page shift, with chunk size as one shifted by that amount and a mask clearing low bits for bucket hashing. Deferred freeing is bounded per work item and paced on a sub-second delay derived from the kernel tick rate.
Hash bucket pairs an intrusive hash chain head for tracked objects with a raw spinlock guarding that chain, forming the unit of concurrent hash access.
Pool statistics record current usage, observed peak usage, and lowest observed global fill level, supporting refill accounting and load estimation.
Pooled object container holds an intrusive list head, live count, low and high watermarks, and embedded usage statistics, with instances aligned to avoid cache-line sharing.

Global pool starts with low watermark at the quarter-fill level and high watermark at full capacity, with minimum-fill statistics initialized to full. The deferred-free pool accepts unbounded intake up to the unsigned maximum and carries no low watermark.

Global hash array is statically sized to the bucket count, and a boot-time object array is statically sized to global capacity and marked as early-init data for use before the slab cache is available.

Batch movement between pools splices exactly one batch unit at a time using a recorded batch tail pointer. Push fails when the destination is at its ceiling, pop fails when the source is empty, and live counts are adjusted by a full batch with ordered stores. Single-object take removes the head entry or reports empty.

Per-CPU allocation requires interrupts disabled and serves from the local cache first. When the local level drops below a near-full threshold at a batch boundary, it opportunistically refills one batch from the deferred pool under the pool lock and updates usage stats. On local exhaustion it takes one batch from deferred then global pools under lock, returning empty only if both are dry.

Background refill first recycles from the deferred pool through a single-flight guarded pass, then allocates fresh batches from the slab cache with high-priority no-warn flags plus conditional reclaim in preemptible or earliest-boot contexts. Allocation concurrency is bounded so only one CPU allocates unless the global level is critical, and overflow batches divert to the deferred pool.

Each hash bucket has its own raw spinlock held with interrupts disabled across lookup, allocation linkage, and drain. A separate global pool lock guards cross-pool batch moves and count checks, taken in refill and free paths that hold no bucket lock, with interrupt-safe variants in allocation and free paths.

Tracked objects move among none, initialized, inactive, active, destroyed and unavailable conditions. Initialization accepts none, initialized or inactive and leaves the object initialized. Any other prior condition triggers an out-of-lock error report and, for previously active objects, an optional descriptor fixup. Fresh allocations start at none, or at initialized for confirmed static objects in assert and activate paths.

When object allocation fails under a held bucket lock, the tracker disables itself globally and, after releasing the lock, drains every bucket into a local list for disposal while warning that tracking is off. Later error printers suppress output once disabled to avoid cascading reports.

Error reporting is rate-limited to a small number of detailed warnings per boot, excludes self-test descriptors, and counts every warning. Stack-annotation mismatches emit a separate capped warning plus a programming alert. Fixup callbacks are invoked only when provided and counted on success.
Bucket selection shifts the object address down by the chunk shift to collapse intra-chunk aliases, then hashes the result into the configured bit width to index the global table.

Usage sampling throttles to roughly ten-millisecond intervals with a trylock-protected average combining current global usage scaled by the per-work free bound. Deferred free work clears its active flag, skips freeing when demand refills the global pool, and otherwise frees a bounded number of batches per pass based on declining average use.
Offline transition for a CPU drains that CPU cache into the shared disposal path while the CPU is already dead, making remote access safe, then resets the local count to empty.
Bucket lookup walks the chain counting examined entries and returns the first object whose address matches. Only unsuccessful searches update the observed maximum chain length.

Boot options enable or disable object tracking before init, backed by a static branch that selects per-CPU slab allocation once the cache exists or a boot list beforehand. Refill is skipped when the global level is healthy, recycles deferred objects first, and allocates fresh memory only when allowed by real-time blocking, preemptibility, scheduling state and interrupt context.

Static-object confirmation delegates to the descriptor predicate with a self-test that reads an embedded flag. Stack placement verification compares actual stack residence against the caller annotation, warning on mismatch. Allocation in assert and activate paths is refused for non-static objects via an error pointer.

Slab batch construction links entries through a shared batch tail and zeroes each object. Any mid-batch allocation failure discards the partial batch and stops the fill loop. Lifetime counters track total allocations and total slab releases.
Object-debug log lines carry a fixed textual prefix identifying the subsystem.

Diagnostic state uses racy-tolerant counters for chain peaks, checked counts, fixups, warnings, allocations and releases, plus a racy enable flag defaulting from build configuration, a self-test descriptor pointer, and a slab cache pointer fixed after init.
Global refill is requested when live count falls below the low watermark and treated as critical when below half that watermark, gating allocation concurrency and background fill decisions.
